Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 61, compiled from the sources I was able to access within the search and fetch limits:

---

## Isaiah 61 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overall Structure and Speaker

The chapter opens with the Messiah Himself speaking (vv. 1–3), then describes the restoration of His people (vv. 4–9), and concludes with the people's joyful response (vv. 10–11).

- **John Gill** (Reformed Baptist, 1746): Both Christ and the church are introduced speaking in turn. It begins with the words of Christ describing His work and office, then the reparation of the church is prophesied, and finally the church rejoices in being clothed with His righteousness.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown)**: Messiah announces His twofold commission — gospel mercy at His first coming, and judgments on unbelievers and comfort to Zion at His second coming (vv. 1–9). The language can be applied to Isaiah comforting the exiles only in a subordinate sense.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott (Anglican)**: We have a new poem in the form of a soliloquy. The Jewish Targum and many modern critics hear only the voice of Isaiah. Guided by the Servant Songs, we recognize the utterance of the ideal Servant of Jehovah. Our Lord's application of the passage to His own work in Luke 4:16–22 confirms the messianic reading for all Christian minds.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

---

### v. 1a — "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me…"

- **Enduring Word (David Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: Isaiah prophetically speaks for the Messiah. Jesus read this passage in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:16–22) and said, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing." Jesus is the one the Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon. If Jesus, the Son of God, needed the Spirit, how much more do we. "Anointed" identifies the speaker as the Messiah ("Messiah" means "Anointed One"). Under the New Covenant, all Christians have an anointing (1 John 2:20) — being filled with and blessed by the Holy Spirit.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **Gill**: No doubt the Messiah Himself is the person speaking, as appears from Luke 4:17. The Spirit of God was on Him — not only grace and gifts, but the person of the Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity. Jehovah the Father was the Anointer of Christ; Christ was anointed from everlasting, being invested with the office of Mediator (Proverbs 8:21), and in the fullness of time at His birth and baptism with the Holy Spirit without measure (Psalm 45:7).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **JFB**: Quoted by Jesus as His credentials in preaching (Luke 4:18–21). The Spirit is upon Him in preaching because Jehovah has anointed Him from the womb (Luke 1:35), and at baptism with the Spirit "without measure," permanently abiding on Him (Isaiah 11:2; John 1:32; 3:34; Psalm 45:7). "Anointed" as Messiah, Prophet, Priest, and King.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: The opening words repeat what was said of the Servant in Isaiah 42:1. The "anointing" might be that of king (1 Sam 9:16; 10:1), or priest (Ex 29:2; Lev 7:36), or prophet (1 Ki 19:16). As interpreted by its fulfilment, it may include all three.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **John MacArthur (Baptist/GTY)**: This is a messianic text. The Messiah Himself is speaking of His own ministry to come, and He says it will be a ministry with the anointing of the Spirit of the Lord. Jesus declared, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing." He is saying, "I am the Messiah."
  — https://www.gty.org/sermons/81-142/salvation-is-for-the-destitute

---

### v. 1b — "to preach good news to the poor… to bind up the brokenhearted… to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners"

- **Enduring Word**: The Messiah announces He is here to heal the damage sin brings. Because sin impoverishes, He preaches good tidings to the poor. Because sin breaks hearts, He heals the brokenhearted. Because sin makes captives, He proclaims liberty to captives and the opening of the prison to those who are bound.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **Gill**: "The meek" or "poor" (as in Luke 4:18) are those sensible of sin and humbled for it, who are sensible of their spiritual poverty and seek the true riches. The Gospel is good tidings concerning the love, grace, and mercy of God; peace, pardon, righteousness, life and salvation. "Brokenhearted" are those whose hearts are smitten by the Spirit and Word of God, cut to the heart, with wounded spirits — Christ binds them up by speaking comfortably, applying His blood, and discovering full pardon. "Captives" are those captive to sin, Satan, and the law.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **JFB**: "Good tidings" is what the word "gospel" means. "The meek" — rather "the poor," those afflicted with calamity, poor in circumstances and in spirit (Matt 11:5). "Proclaim liberty" — language drawn from the deliverance of the Babylonian captives and from the liberty proclaimed in the year of jubilee (Lev 25:10). "Opening of the prison" — the Hebrew is "the most complete opening," namely of the eyes to them that are bound (Ewald). The Septuagint (and Luke 4:18) renders it "recovery of sight to the blind."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: "To bind up the broken-hearted" — the primary thought is a healing bandage applied to the heart's wounds. The Servant of Jehovah is the great physician as well as the evangelist. "To proclaim liberty" — phrase and thought from the Year of Jubilee (Lev 25:10). "The opening of the prison" — the LXX, adopted in Luke 4:18, gives "recovery of sight to the blind"; the verb is never used for opening a door, and is used in Isaiah 35:5 and 42:7 for opening of the eyes, so that is probably its meaning.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **MacArthur (Baptist)**: The good news is only good news if you understand the bad reality of the sinner's condition. "Poor" (Greek *ptōchos*) means utter destitution — spiritual bankruptcy. "Captives" are prisoners of war in exile awaiting execution; Messiah brings forgiveness and deliverance. "Blind" are those in spiritual darkness. "Oppressed" are those downtrodden under sin and guilt. The only people for whom this is good news are the destitute — poor, prisoners, blind, and oppressed. All evangelism begins with recognition of the human condition.
  — https://www.gty.org/sermons/81-142/salvation-is-for-the-destitute

- **Spurgeon (Baptist)**: Christ proclaims liberty even to poor, wretched bond-slaves of sin fettered with iron chains of despair. "Trust him, and you shall be freed from sin, and walk at large — your Saviour's blood your full discharge." There is a general discharge of prisoners; Christ died to make it possible and lives to perfect the emancipation of all for whom He died.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-61-commentary

---

### v. 2 — "to proclaim the year of the LORD's favor and the day of our God's vengeance, to comfort all who mourn"

- **Enduring Word**: Because sin is a crime that must be avenged, He will proclaim the day of vengeance. Significantly, Jesus stopped reading before this sentence in Luke 4 — the day of vengeance belongs to His Second Coming, not His first. The comma between "the year of the LORD's favor" and "the day of vengeance" has stood for nearly 2,000 years. Biblical prophecy may "shift gears" and time frames quickly and without warning. We can compare a whole year of grace to a single day of vengeance.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: "Acceptable year" — the year of jubilee on which liberty was proclaimed (2 Cor 6:2). The "acceptable time of grace" is a "year"; the time of "vengeance" but "a day" (Isa 34:8; 63:4; Mal 4:1). Jesus "closed the book" before the vengeance clause; the interval from His first to His second coming is the acceptable year. "Our God" — the saints call Him so because He comes to avenge them (Rev 6:10; 19:2).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Gill**: "The acceptable year of the Lord" alludes to the year of jubilee. Jarchi interprets it as "a year of reconciliation." The whole time of Christ on earth, and the entire Gospel dispensation, is the acceptable year. "The day of vengeance of our God" — when vengeance was taken on sin in the person of Christ; when He destroyed the works of the devil; when He brought wrath on the Jews for rejecting Him; and when He will take vengeance on antichrist and all the wicked at the day of judgment.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: The Year of Jubilee is still in the prophet's thoughts. The chief point is the contrast between the "year" of favour and the single "day" of vengeance, reminding us of the contrast in Exodus 20:5–6.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **MacArthur (Baptist/GTY)**: Jesus stopped halfway through Isaiah 61:2 because the last half — "the day of vengeance of our God" — is future. This is not the day of vengeance; this is the day of salvation.
  — https://www.gty.org/sermons/81-142/salvation-is-for-the-destitute

---

### v. 3 — "to console the mourners in Zion — to give them a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified."

- **Enduring Word**: The Messiah's comfort is specific and lavish: beauty instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning, a garment of praise instead of heaviness. "Why do we sit in the ashes, why do we mourn, why do we indulge the spirit of heaviness when Jesus gave us something so much better?" The word "beauty" means a beautiful crown or head ornament (translated "exquisite hats" in Ex 39:28 and "headdresses" in Isa 3:20). In mourning, ashes were cast on the head (2 Sam 13:19); here ashes are replaced with a beautiful crown. "Trees of righteousness" — God's people are as strong, beautiful, and useful as trees. When people look at them, they see they are the planting of the LORD.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: There is a play on the sound and meaning of the Hebrew words *peer* and *epher* — "ornamental headdress" or tiara (Ezek 24:17), worn in times of joy, instead of a headdress of "ashes" cast on the head in mourning (2 Sam 13:19). "Oil of joy" — perfumed ointment poured on guests at joyous feasts (Ps 23:5; 45:7–8); on occasions of grief its use was laid aside (2 Sam 14:2). "Garment of praise" — bright-colored garments of thankfulness instead of sackcloth. "Trees of righteousness" — Hebrew *terebinth trees*, symbolical of men strong in righteousness instead of being bowed down as a reed with sin and calamity.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Gill**: There is a beautiful wordplay in the Hebrew — "to give *peer* for *epher*." In times of mourning it was usual to put on sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:1). Instead, Christ gives the beautiful garments of salvation, the robe of His righteousness, the graces of His Spirit, and His gracious presence. "Oil of joy" — the grace of the Spirit, called "the oil of gladness" (Ps 45:7). "Trees of righteousness" — trees well planted, whose root is in Christ, whose sap is the Spirit and His grace, and whose fruit are good works; truly righteous persons made so by the imputation of Christ's righteousness.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: "Beauty for ashes" — literally a diadem or coronet to replace the ashes sprinkled on the head of mourners or penitents (2 Sam 1:2; 13:19; Josh 7:6). The assonance of *'epher* and *paer* deserves notice. "The spirit of heaviness" — the word is that used for the "dimly burning" flax in Isa 42:3. "Trees of righteousness" — strictly terebinths or oaks, symbols of perennial verdure; the "righteousness" is the gift of the Spirit of Jehovah, life-giving and enduring, and in their beauty and strength manifesting His glory.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Spurgeon (Baptist)**: The Lord acts on terms of exchange or barter — He gives beauty for ashes, oil of joy for mourning, a garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. In condescending compassion He took our ashes upon Himself. "Ah, how they once covered his sacred head and marred his beauty!" He took our mourning and became the man of sorrows. He took our spirit of heaviness and lay prostrate in the garden, exceeding sorrowful unto death. It is a barter in which there is double profit on our side — we lose a loss, and the gain is pure gain. The way believers rise out of mourning is through the coming of Jesus. "Look thou, O sinner, always to the brazen serpent whatever serpent bites thee."
  — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/beauty-for-ashes

---

### v. 4 — "They will rebuild the ancient ruins; they will restore the places long devastated; they will renew the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations."

- **Enduring Word**: God loves to restore ruins. He wants to use His people to restore and rebuild things broken down and ruined. Even if the rubble has stood for many generations, God can still use His people to rebuild. A partial fulfillment is Nehemiah rebuilding Jerusalem's decades-old rubble.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **Gill**: This was literally true when the Jews returned from Babylon. But it more fully respects the spiritual building of the church in Gospel times and especially the latter-day restoration of the Jews, when the tabernacle of David that is fallen down will be rebuilt (Amos 9:11).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **JFB**: "Old wastes" — Jerusalem and the cities of Judah which long lay in ruins.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: Not merely cities ruined during the exile, but those lying waste for generations — parallel with Isaiah 58:12. The rebuilding is Israel's own work, while service of another kind is assigned to aliens (v. 5).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

---

### v. 5 — "Strangers will stand and feed your flocks, and foreigners will be your plowmen and vinedressers."

- **JFB**: "Stand" — shall wait on you as servants (Isa 14:1–2; 60:10).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: Like servants waiting for their master's orders. The implied thought of the whole passage is that all Israel is raised to the dignity of a priestly caste, leaving the rough work of the world to foreigners on a lower level.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Gill**: The several congregated churches of Christ, compared to flocks of sheep, shall be fed with knowledge and understanding by pastors of the Gentile race. The "sons of the alien" — converted Gentiles, once aliens from the commonwealth of Israel (Eph 2:12) — will be of eminent service in His church; the church is "God's husbandry" (1 Cor 3:9) and they shall cultivate it with the plough of the Gospel.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

---

### v. 6 — "But you will be called the priests of the LORD; they will speak of you as ministers of our God; you will feed on the wealth of nations, and you will boast in their riches."

- **JFB**: As contrasted with the "strangers," you shall have no need to attend to flocks and lands — strangers will do that. Your exclusive business will be the service of Jehovah as His "priests" (Exodus 19:6, yet to be realized; compare 1 Pet 2:5, 9; Rev 1:6; 5:10).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: This had been the original ideal of the nation's life (Ex 19:6), forfeited for a time through sin (Ex 28:1), to be fulfilled at last in the citizens of the new Jerusalem (compare 1 Pet 2:9). As Israel succeeds to the position of the sons of Aaron, so mankind at large occupies the position of Israel as chosen and redeemed. Even the heathen Gentiles shall speak of the new Israel as "Ministers of our God." St. Paul seems to see a partial fulfilment in the collection made among the Gentiles for the Jerusalem church (Rom 15:27).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Gill**: This particularly designates the Jews when converted — there will no longer be a distinction of priests and common people, but all shall be kings and priests unto God, a royal priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices. "Ye shall eat the riches of the Gentiles" — converted Gentiles shall bring their wealth and support the interest of Christ (see Isa 60:5), or it may be understood of spiritual riches, the unsearchable riches of Christ revealed in the Gospel.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

---

### v. 7 — "Instead of shame, My people will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation, they will rejoice in their share; and so they will inherit a double portion in their land, and everlasting joy will be theirs."

- **Enduring Word**: What a change under the anointing of the Spirit and the ministry of the Messiah! No more shame; now double honor. No more confusion; they shall rejoice in their portion. Everlasting joy shall be theirs — a joy that can never be taken away.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: "Double" — instead of your past share, you shall have not merely as much but double as much reward (Isa 40:2; Zech 9:12). "In their land" — marking the reference to literal Israel, not to the Church at large.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: Double compensation for the suffering of years (comp. Zech 9:12), the general idea passing into a double inheritance of territory.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Gill**: "For your shame you shall have double" — instead of being a reproach and a curse as the Jews now are everywhere, being converted they will have double honour in things civil and religious. They shall rejoice in Christ their portion and all spiritual blessings. "In their land they shall possess the double" — not only in the land of the Gentiles where they suffered reproach, but in their own land, the land of Israel, to which they shall be restored.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

---

### v. 8 — "For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity; in My faithfulness I will give them their recompense and make an everlasting covenant with them."

- **Enduring Word**: The LORD explains that sacrifices such as a burnt offering can really just amount to robbery if the heart isn't right. Instead, the LORD loves justice. Sacrifices alone, and the sacrificial system in itself, are not enough. God has an alternative: He will direct their work in truth and make an everlasting covenant.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: "Judgment" — justice, which requires that I should restore My people and give them double in compensation. "Robbery for burnt offering" — rather "the spoil of iniquity" (Horsley), as in Job 5:6. Hating the rapine combined with iniquity perpetrated on My people, I will vindicate Israel.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: The AV follows the Vulgate and Luther, but the words commonly applied as condemning the formal sacrifices of the wicked do not fit the context. It is better to take the LXX and Targum rendering: "I hate robbery with violence," referring to the spoliation Israel suffered at the hands of the Chaldæans. "I will direct their work in truth" — better, "I will appoint their recompense in faithfulness."
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Gill**: The Lord loves judgment — to do what is right Himself and to see it done by others; therefore He will right the wrongs of His people. He loves strict justice and will not be put off with an imperfect or hypocritical righteousness; only the perfect righteousness of Christ satisfies. "I hate robbery for burnt offering" — that which is stolen, though converted into a burnt offering; all immorality along with ceremonial sacrifices, as if it could be atoned for by them.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

---

### v. 9 — "Their descendants will be known among the nations, and their offspring among the peoples. All who see them will acknowledge that they are a people the LORD has blessed."

- **Enduring Word**: This everlasting covenant brings blessings so prominent that the blessed shall be known among the Gentiles; all who see them shall acknowledge them. The writer to the Hebrews pronounces a blessing regarding this everlasting covenant (Heb 13:20–21).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: "Known" — honorably; shall be illustrious (Ps 67:2).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: Their seed shall be "renowned" or honourably recognized, even by the heathen, as the people whom Jehovah has blessed (comp. Isa 65:23).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

---

### v. 10 — "I will rejoice greatly in the LORD, my soul will exult in my God; for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels."

- **Enduring Word**: The blessed one's joy isn't in the blessing itself but in the LORD — the same thought expressed in Philippians 4:4. The granting of salvation and righteousness is represented by clothing — glorious garments, as a bridegroom decks himself with ornaments and as a bride adorns herself with jewels. These are given garments: "He has clothed me… He has covered me."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: Zion (v. 3) gives thanks for God's returning favour (compare Luke 1:46–47; Hab 3:18). "Salvation… righteousness" — inseparably connected together. The "robe" is a loose mantle thrown over the other parts of the dress (Ps 132:9, 16; 149:4; Rev 21:2; 19:8). The bridegroom "decketh himself with ornaments" — rather "maketh himself a priestly headdress," a magnificent headdress such as worn by the high priest (a mitre and a plate or crown of gold), appropriate to the "kingdom of priests" (Ex 19:6; Rev 5:10; 20:6).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: The speaker is again the ideal Servant of Jehovah, who identifies Himself with the people. The Targum makes Jerusalem the speaker. The imagery is the same as Isaiah 59:17 and v. 3, its entirely spiritual significance being still more strongly accentuated. The bridegroom wears a turban (or mitre), as a priest; it appears from Song 3:11 that bridegrooms wore a special head-dress on the day of their espousal, compared to the priestly "bonnet" or "mitre" (Ex 28:4; 39:28; Ezek 44:18).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **MacArthur (Baptist/GTY)**: This verse is a marvelous declaration: God clothed us with garments of salvation and covered us with the robe of righteousness. God did it.
  — https://www.gty.org/sermons/45-30/how-to-be-right-with-god-part-2

---

### v. 11 — "For as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden enables seed to spring up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations."

- **Enduring Word**: The blessing of God grows — it isn't manufactured but grows. We can never make something grow; the blessing of life is miraculously within the seed. But we can provide the right environment for the seed to bud, grow, and be fruitful. That's how we receive and flourish in God's blessings — we put our hearts and minds in the right environments of faith, fellowship, and obedience.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **JFB**: Compares with Isaiah 45:8; 55:10–11; Psalm 72:3; 85:11.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Ellicott**: The passage is memorable as at least suggesting the leading thought of the parable of the sower, and the appropriation of that title to Himself by the Son of Man (Matt 13:3–23, 37; Mark 4:26–29).
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Gill**: This is the church's confidence that her righteousness and glory will appear before all nations. As surely as the earth brings forth her bud and the garden causes seed to spring up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring forth — an illustrious prophecy.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### The Identity of the Speaker in v. 1

There is a notable divergence on whether vv. 1–3 are exclusively the voice of the Messiah, or whether the prophet Isaiah (or the "ideal Servant") also speaks in a subordinate sense.

- **Traditional Reformed / Baptist (Gill, JFB)**: The speaker is unequivocally the Messiah. Gill notes that the Targum, Aben Ezra, and Kimchi attributed the words to the prophet, but "there is no doubt but the Messiah himself is the person speaking, as appears from Luke 4:17."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **Anglican (Ellicott)**: Holds a both/and view. The Jewish Targum and many modern critics hear only the voice of Isaiah. Guided by the Servant Songs, we recognise the "ideal Servant of Jehovah." Our Lord's application confirms the messianic reading, but the historical application to the prophet is acknowledged.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **JFB** similarly notes that the language "can be applied to Isaiah, comforting by his prophecies the exiles in Babylon, only in a subordinate sense."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

### The Scope of Restoration (vv. 4–9): Literal Israel or the Church?

- **JFB (Reformed, older)**: Marks "in their land" (v. 7) as "marking the reference to literal Israel, not to the Church at large." The restoration includes a literal return to the land.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist, older)**: Holds a both/and view — literal fulfilment in the return from Babylon, but ultimate fulfilment in Gospel church-building and the future conversion of the Jews. He sees "strangers feeding your flocks" as Gentile pastors and the entire passage as pointing to the latter-day calling of the Jews.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: Applies the rebuilding language broadly to the church — God loves to restore ruins through His people. Nehemiah is a partial fulfillment; the promise applies to any believer whom God uses "to repair what has been broken for generations."
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/

- **Ellicott (Anglican)**: Sees the rebuilding as "Israel's own work" and applies v. 6's priesthood language as fulfilled "at last in the citizens of the new Jerusalem" (1 Pet 2:9), with Paul seeing partial fulfilment in the Gentile collection for Jerusalem (Rom 15:27). He holds the "both/and" tension in prophetic imagery.
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

### "Robbery for burnt offering" (v. 8)

- **Reformed/Anglican (JFB, Ellicott)**: Prefer the translation "spoil of iniquity" or "robbery with violence," referring to the plundering Israel suffered from enemies.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-61.html
  — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/61.htm

- **Baptist (Gill), Pentecostal (Enduring Word)**: Read it as condemning hypocritical worship — stolen goods offered as sacrifices, or sacrifices without a right heart.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-61.html
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-61/
